pos: n. (town at the mouth of the Meuse, English the Brill; taken by the Sea Beggars on the first of April 1572, and where the Gorcum clergy were hanged in July)
etymology: Dutch Brielle, from a Germanic root brida or bril, a narrow place or a strip of land; the town guards the mouth of the Meuse.
biblical_def: Brielle was a small walled town at the mouth of the Meuse, and on the first of April 1572 a fleet of the exiled privateers called the Sea Beggars, driven out of English harbours and short of provisions, put in and found it undefended. They took it and held it, and because they held it the revolt of the Netherlands had a base on Dutch soil; within three months Flushing, Enkhuizen and most of the towns of Holland and Zeeland had declared for the prince of Orange. The date is kept in Dutch memory as the beginning of the Republic. Three months later the same town was the scene of something else. Nineteen Roman clergy—Franciscans, a parish priest and others—seized when the Beggars took Gorinchem, were brought down to Brielle, pressed to renounce the papal supremacy and the doctrine of the Supper, refused, and were hanged in a turf shed on the ninth of July 1572. Rome canonised them in 1867 as the Martyrs of Gorcum. The dictionary enters Brielle with both facts in one entry, because they belong in one entry, and because a church which will only record the persecutions it suffered has not told the truth about itself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a privateer as a private ship commissioned to seize an enemy's vessels; a martyr as one who suffers death for his faith; and revolt as a casting off of allegiance.
webster_full: PRIVATEER, n. A ship or vessel of war owned and equipped by a private man, but authorized by a commission to cruise against the enemy.
MARTYR, n. [Gr. a witness.] One who suffers death in defense of the Christian faith, or in defense of any belief whatever.
REVOLT, n. [Fr. revolte.] Desertion; change of sides; a casting off allegiance to a prince or state; an insurrection.
RENOUNCE, v.t. [L. renuncio.] To disown; to reject; to disclaim; to abandon a profession or a doctrine formerly held.
SHED, n. A slight or temporary building; a penthouse; a hut for the shelter of cattle or for storing turf or tools.

corruption_summary: Meuse town taken by the Sea Beggars in April 1572, giving the revolt its first base, and where nineteen Roman clergy were hanged in July.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named here is on the Protestant side, and the dictionary names it without mitigation. The nineteen men hanged at Brielle were prisoners; they were killed for refusing to renounce the doctrine of their church; and that is persecution whoever does it and whatever the doctrine. The Reformed cause was not advanced by it and was disgraced by it, and “yea, the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service” (Joh 16:2) applies to the men who built that gallows as exactly as to the court at Pozsony.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary holds the doctrines the Gorcum clergy died rather than deny to be error—the papal supremacy and the sacrifice of the Mass—and holds equally that they should not have died. Those two statements are not in conflict and the refusal to make both of them is what makes most confessional history worthless. “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Rom 12:19) is the rule that was broken at Brielle in July, by men who had been delivered at Brielle in April.

pos: n. (town on the Merwede, English Gorcum; taken by the Sea Beggars in 1572, whence the Gorcum clergy were carried to Brielle)
etymology: Dutch Gorinchem, earlier Gorichem, from a personal name Goric and the Germanic heim, a home; the town stands where the Linge enters the Merwede.
biblical_def: Gorinchem is a fortified town on the Merwede at the junction of the great rivers, and in the summer of 1572 it was one of the places which fell to the Sea Beggars as the revolt spread inland from Brielle. When the town was taken its religious were seized: the Franciscans of the house there, the parish priest and his curate, and a number of other clergy from the neighbourhood, nineteen in all. They were held, interrogated, offered their liberty if they would renounce the pope's supremacy and the doctrine of transubstantiation, and when they would not, they were sent down the river to Brielle and hanged. The town itself was held for the States thereafter and was a Reformed town of the Republic. The dictionary enters Gorinchem beside Brielle because the seizure happened here and the hanging there, and because the whole episode makes a point about the revolt which its Protestant historians have been slow to make. The Dutch rising was a war of liberation and it was also a war, conducted by irregular troops with old scores, and the men who began the Republic began it with a crime.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a friar as a brother of a religious order; interrogation as the act of questioning; and irregular as not according to rule or discipline.
webster_full: FRIAR, n. [Fr. frere, a brother.] An appellation common to the monks of all orders; a brother of a religious order.
INTERROGATION, n. The act of questioning; a question put; examination by questions.
IRREGULAR, adj. [L. irregularis.] Not according to rule or established principle; not conformable to discipline, as irregular troops.
CURATE, n. [L. curatus.] A clergyman employed to perform the duties of another; one who has the cure of souls.
LIBERATION, n. [L. liberatio.] The act of setting free; deliverance from restraint, bondage or oppression.

corruption_summary: Merwede town taken by the Sea Beggars in 1572, where nineteen Roman clergy were seized and sent to Brielle to be hanged.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the killing of prisoners for their religion, and the dictionary has named it at Brielle and names it again here because the seizure is the part the Reformed accounts pass over. The men were taken because of what they were, held while an offer was made which only their religion prevented them from accepting, and then killed. That is the exact structure of a religious execution, and the fact that it was carried out by irregulars rather than by a court does not improve it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one that applies when a church's own side is in the wrong. “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3) does not say that the prisoners to be remembered are of our own confession, and the Dutch Reformed who had themselves been hunted for thirty years were under a double obligation here, which they broke. The dictionary records it as a crime and declines to balance it against the Spanish massacres at Naarden and Zutphen: both were crimes, and a ledger is not an argument.

pos: n. (fortified town on the Zuiderzee; its inhabitants massacred by the Spanish army on the first of December 1572)
etymology: Dutch Naarden, from a Germanic root nard or naar, a narrow or wet place; the town stands on the southern shore of the Zuiderzee east of Amsterdam.
biblical_def: Naarden was a small walled town on the Zuiderzee which had declared for the prince of Orange in the summer of 1572. When Don Fadrique, the son of the Duke of Alva, came north with the Spanish army to recover Holland, Naarden was the first place in his way. The town, having no hope of holding out, sent out deputies and surrendered on terms. The terms were not kept. The troops were admitted, the inhabitants were assembled in the hospital chapel and in the streets, and the greater part of the population was killed; the town was burned and its walls thrown down. The number is variously given and was certainly in the high hundreds. The massacre was intended as an example and was published as one, and in the short run it worked: Haarlem was frightened, and Amsterdam was confirmed in its loyalty. In the longer run it did the opposite, for after Naarden no town in Holland believed a Spanish promise, which is a chief reason Haarlem held seven months and Alkmaar and Leiden held at all. The dictionary enters Naarden as the plainest case in the war of a terror which achieved the contrary of its purpose.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines terror as extreme fear, that which excites dread; capitulation as the act of surrendering on stipulated terms; and faith as the observance of a promise.
webster_full: TERROR, n. [L. terror.] Extreme fear; violent dread; fright; that which may excite dread; the cause of extreme fear.
CAPITULATION, n. The act of capitulating or surrendering to an enemy upon stipulated terms; the treaty or instrument containing the conditions.
FAITH, n. Fidelity; the observance of a promise or a treaty; the keeping of one's word; as to break faith.
EXAMPLE, n. [L. exemplum.] A pattern; a copy; one or a portion selected to show the character of the whole; a warning.
MASSACRE, n. The slaughter of numbers of human beings with cruelty or without necessity.

corruption_summary: Zuiderzee town whose population was massacred by the Spanish army in December 1572 after surrendering on terms, as a published example.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is terror used as a policy of state, with a broken capitulation as its instrument. The killing at Naarden was not the collapse of discipline in a storming; the town had surrendered and the troops were admitted by agreement. A government which does this has decided that the fear of its subjects is worth more than their belief in its word, and it then finds that nobody will ever again surrender to it on terms.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providential one, stated carefully. “And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God” (Rom 8:28) is true of Naarden, and what it means is not that the massacre was a blessing or that the dead were a price. It means that God governs even the counsels of the cruel, and that the example meant to break Holland was the thing which made the next three towns impossible to persuade. The dead did not consent to that use of their deaths; God made it, and the comfort of the text belongs to the living.

pos: n. (Hanseatic town on the Yssel in Gelderland; sacked with great slaughter by the Spanish army in November 1572)
etymology: Dutch Zutphen, from zuid, south, and veen, a fen or peat moor—the south fen; the town stands where the Berkel enters the Yssel.
biblical_def: Zutphen was an old Hanseatic town on the Yssel, one of the places of the Devotio Moderna in the fifteenth century and a town of the revolt in 1572. When Don Fadrique moved north in November of that year Zutphen was taken and sacked, and the slaughter there was on the same scale and the same principle as at Naarden a few weeks later: the garrison and a great part of the townspeople were killed, some drowned in the Yssel, and the event was published to frighten the other towns of the north-east. Zutphen afterwards changed hands several times in the long war; it was retaken by the States in 1591. Its church history has the double character of all these Yssel towns—a strong late-medieval piety of the Brethren of the Common Life, with their schools and their libraries, giving way in a generation to a Reformed church which inherited the buildings and some of the habits. The dictionary enters Zutphen because the two things stand together in one town: the chained library of the chapter, where townsmen were reading for themselves in the fifteenth century, and the market place where the Spanish army killed them in the sixteenth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a sack as the pillage of a town taken by storm; a garrison as a body of troops stationed in a fort; and a library as a collection of books.
webster_full: SACK, n. The pillage or plunder of a town or city, or the storm and plunder of a town; devastation; waste.
GARRISON, n. [Fr. garnison.] A body of troops stationed in a fort or fortified town for its defense.
LIBRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a person or to an institution; a building appropriated for such a collection.
HANSEATIC, adj. Pertaining to the Hanse towns, or to their confederacy for the protection of commerce.
CHAIN, v.t. To fasten with a chain; to fasten a book to a desk, as in old libraries.

corruption_summary: Yssel town of the Brethren's schools and libraries, sacked with great slaughter by the Spanish army in November 1572.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the sack as an instrument of government, and the dictionary adds one observation about the men who ordered it. They were not barbarians and they were not ignorant; they were the officers of the most sophisticated monarchy in Europe, acting on a reasoned policy approved at Brussels and Madrid, and they expected to be understood. Atrocity in a war of religion is characteristically a policy rather than a frenzy, and that is the fact most accounts obscure.

The principle to recover is the continuity of a town's own history, which these entries make visible. The chained books of the Zutphen chapter and the Reformed pulpit of the next century are the same story: “they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) was being learned here before Luther, and the people who had learned it were the people the army killed.

pos: n. (small town of Holland on the Hollandse Yssel; stormed and its people killed by the Spanish army in August 1575)
etymology: Dutch Oudewater, the old water, from oud, old, and water; the town stands on the Hollandse Yssel west of Utrecht.
biblical_def: Oudewater is a very small town of Holland on the Hollandse Yssel, and in August 1575 it was stormed by the Spanish army under Hierges after a short siege and the greater part of its inhabitants were killed or carried off; the town was burned. It was the last of the massacres of the Dutch war and it was done on the same principle as Naarden three years earlier, with the same purpose and the same result, which is to say none. By 1575 the towns of Holland had already discovered at Haarlem, Alkmaar and Leiden what a Spanish promise was worth and what a flooded polder could do to an army, and the destruction of a town of a few thousand people altered nothing. The dictionary enters Oudewater partly to complete the record and partly for one further reason. It is the smallest and least known of these places, its name is not in the national mythology beside Alkmaar and Leiden, and almost everybody in it died; which is a reasonably good description of the circumstances of most of the people the church has ever lost, and an argument for keeping registers that do not only record the famous.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to storm as to assault a fortified place; obscure as unnoticed, not known to fame; and a register as a book of record preserved as evidence.
webster_full: STORM, v.t. To assault; to attack and attempt to take by scaling walls, forcing gates or breaches.
OBSCURE, adj. [L. obscurus.] Not noticed; unknown to fame; unnoticed; humble; mean; not easily understood.

POLDER, n. In the Netherlands, a tract of low land reclaimed from the water and protected by dykes.

corruption_summary: The smallest and least remembered of the Dutch war's massacred towns, stormed and destroyed in August 1575 to no military purpose.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the same policy of terror, and by 1575 it had the added character of futility: it had been tried three times and had three times produced the opposite of its aim, and it was tried again. The dictionary notes that this is the usual career of such policies. They are not abandoned when they fail, because the men who adopt them have no other method and cannot admit that the method is the problem.

The principle to recover is the keeping of the obscure. “To hear the groaning of the prisoner; to loose those that are appointed to death” (Psa 102:20) is said of God hearing people whose names no chronicle holds. “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant” (Isa 1:9) is the right frame for a town where almost everyone died. The dictionary holds that a church's register of its own losses should be kept by place and by name, and that the places which have no part in a national story are exactly the ones that will otherwise be lost.

pos: n. (town of Holland on the Oude Rijn; birthplace of Jan de Bakker, the first Dutch Protestant martyr, burned in 1525)
etymology: Dutch Woerden, from werd or woerd, a raised dwelling-mound above the river land; the town stands on the Old Rhine between Utrecht and Leiden.
biblical_def: Woerden is a small town on the Old Rhine, and its chief claim on the dictionary is a man. Jan de Bakker, known in Latin as Johannes Pistorius, was born here about 1499, was ordained priest, and came by reading to the evangelical faith; he married, which under the canon law of the time was itself a capital irregularity for a priest, continued to preach, was arrested, examined at Utrecht and The Hague, and was burned at The Hague in September 1525. He is reckoned the first Protestant martyr of the northern Netherlands. The accounts of his examination and death were printed and circulated, and he was sung about; the Dutch martyr literature, which became one of the most powerful instruments of the Reformation in that country, begins substantially with him. Woerden itself was a frontier fortress in the long war, held and besieged more than once, and a Reformed town of the Republic. The dictionary enters it for the man and for what followed from him. The Dutch Reformation was carried less by princes than by printed accounts of ordinary people's deaths, read aloud in households; and the first of those accounts was about a baker's son from this town.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a martyrology as a register of martyrs; celibacy as the state of being unmarried; and to circulate as to pass from hand to hand.
webster_full: MARTYROLOGY, n. [Gr. a witness, and discourse.] A history or account of martyrs with their sufferings; a register of martyrs.
CELIBACY, n. [L. caelebs.] An unmarried state; a single life; applied chiefly to the single state of the clergy.
CIRCULATE, v.i. To move in a circle; to pass from place to place or from hand to hand, as a report or a book.
HOUSEHOLD, n. Those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family; domestic life.
BAKER, n. One whose occupation is to bake bread, biscuit or other articles of food.

corruption_summary: Old Rhine town, birthplace of Jan de Bakker, the first Protestant martyr of the northern Netherlands, burned at The Hague in 1525.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the forbidding of marriage to ministers and the making of a marriage into a capital matter. Jan de Bakker's offences were preaching the evangelical doctrine and taking a wife, and the second was pressed against him with the first. The apostle, having foretold a departure from the faith in the latter times, names among its marks those “Forbidding to marry” (1Ti 4:3), and the dictionary applies the text where the apostle put it: a required clerical celibacy is not a discipline but a doctrine of devils, and the law which burned this man was its enforcement.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the household use of the martyrologies. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16) was fulfilled in the Netherlands partly by families reading printed accounts of the deaths of their neighbours, which taught a whole people what the doctrine cost and therefore what it was worth. “they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11) is the text those books were written under.

pos: n. (herring port on the Zuiderzee; the first town of Holland to declare openly for the prince of Orange, in May 1572)
etymology: Dutch Enkhuizen, from enk, a single or lone, and huizen, houses—the lone houses; the town stands on the point of the Zuiderzee.
biblical_def: Enkhuizen was a herring port and shipbuilding town on the point of the Zuiderzee, and in May 1572, a few weeks after Brielle was taken, its people turned out the Spanish garrison's officers, refused the new citadel the government was building, and declared for the prince of Orange. It was the first town of Holland proper to do so of its own motion, and it mattered far beyond its size, because Enkhuizen's fishing and merchant fleet, with the fleets of Hoorn and Medemblik, gave the revolt command of the Zuiderzee; the Spanish squadron was beaten there in October 1573, and the northern quarter of Holland was never recovered. The town's Reformed congregation was organised at once and its ministers were among those who shaped the church order of the province. The dictionary enters Enkhuizen because it is the clearest instance in the revolt of a town moving before it was safe to move. Brielle was taken by a fleet from outside; Enkhuizen decided for itself, with the Duke of Alva's army intact and the outcome entirely unknown, which is what the word confession means when it is not merely a word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a citadel as a fortress commanding a city; to declare as to make known publicly; and a fleet as a company of ships.
webster_full: CITADEL, n. [It. cittadella.] A fortress in or near a city, intended for its defense, and as a place of retreat, or to command the city.
DECLARE, v.t. [L. declaro.] To make known; to tell explicitly; to manifest or communicate plainly to others by words.
FLEET, n. [Sax. flota.] A navy or squadron of ships; a number of ships in company, whether of war or of commerce.
HERRING, n. A small fish of the genus Clupea, which inhabits the northern seas in vast shoals.
GARRISON, n. A body of troops stationed in a fort or fortified town.

corruption_summary: Zuiderzee herring port, the first town of Holland to declare for Orange of its own motion, in May 1572, with the outcome wholly unknown.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is retrospective courage: the reading of the Dutch revolt backwards from its success, so that the towns which declared in 1572 appear to have joined a winning cause. They did not. The Duke of Alva had an intact army and the finest infantry in Europe, the English and French were unreliable, and the prince of Orange had been beaten twice. What Enkhuizen did in May 1572 was to risk the fate Naarden suffered in December.

The principle to recover is that a confession is made before the result is known. “For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake” (Phi 1:29) puts the suffering in the gift, which is a hard saying and is the plain sense. “they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11) is said of men who had not yet seen how it would end. Reading history backwards is the surest way to learn nothing from it.

pos: n. (port of North Holland on the Zuiderzee; a town of the revolt from 1572 and a base of the fleet that won the Zuiderzee)
etymology: Dutch Hoorn, a horn, from the hook or spit of land on which the harbour was built; the town gave its name to Cape Horn through its merchants.
biblical_def: Hoorn was one of the great ports of North Holland, rich on the Baltic trade, the herring fishery and later on the East India traffic, and it went over to the prince of Orange in the summer of 1572 with Enkhuizen and the other Zuiderzee towns. Its ships were in the squadron which beat the Spanish fleet on the Zuiderzee in October 1573 and took its admiral, an action which secured the northern quarter of Holland for the revolt and is rightly ranked with the land defences of Haarlem and Alkmaar. Hoorn's Reformed congregation was established at once, and the town afterwards had a Latin school and a vigorous consistory. It also had, as a trading port, the ordinary problem of such places: a church whose leading members were merchants in a town whose prosperity came to depend on a company trading in slaves and on wars fought in the East Indies, and a consistory which had to decide how much of that it would examine. The dictionary enters Hoorn because the question is a real one and has never gone away. A congregation of prosperous traders must either apply the law of God to the trade or be an ornament of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines commerce as an interchange of goods between nations; a company as an association of persons for a joint concern; and covetousness as an inordinate desire of gain.
webster_full: COMMERCE, n. An interchange or mutual change of goods, wares or merchandise between nations or individuals; trade; traffick.
COMPANY, n. An association of persons for the purpose of carrying on some commercial or industrial undertaking.
COVETOUSNESS, n. A strong or inordinate desire of obtaining and possessing some supposed good; an eagerness for gain.
FISHERY, n. The business of catching fish; a place for catching fish with nets or hooks.
CONSISTORY, n. An assembly of ecclesiastical persons for the regulation of church affairs; a church court.

corruption_summary: North Holland port of the revolt from 1572, whose fleet won the Zuiderzee, and whose consistory had to judge the trade its members lived by.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the church that will not examine the business of its own leading men. The Dutch ports grew rich in the seventeenth century on commerce which included the traffic in slaves and the armed monopoly of the Indies, and the consistories of those towns were composed in large part of the men who held the shares. “For the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10) is not a text about the poor, and “Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth” (Jam 5:4) is addressed to employers by name.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the discipline of a church must reach the men who pay for it. A consistory which disciplines a servant for drunkenness and cannot ask a director how his cargo was obtained has not got discipline at all; it has a police for the poor. “the priest's lips should keep knowledge” (Mal 2:7) includes the knowledge of what the law of God says about a trade, and the courage to say it where it will cost the collection.

“the priest's lips should keep knowledge” (Mal 2:7) — and the courage to say it where it will cost the collection.

pos: n. (town of North Holland; the first siege of the Dutch war which the Spanish army failed to take, in the autumn of 1573)
etymology: Dutch Alkmaar, from alk, a water-bird, and meer, a lake—the auk lake; the town stands among the North Holland polders.
biblical_def: Alkmaar is a town of North Holland among the polders, and in the autumn of 1573 it was the first place in the war which the Spanish army besieged and did not take. Haarlem had fallen a few months before after seven months and a capitulation which the victors did not honour, and the army came north to Alkmaar expecting the same. The town was small, its walls were old, and its garrison was a few companies with the townspeople; it held through a bombardment and a general assault, and when the States opened the sluices and let the sea into the surrounding polders the Spanish camp was flooded and the siege was raised in October. The Dutch proverb that victory begins at Alkmaar dates from the event and is substantially true: nothing after it went as the army in Brussels planned, and Leiden was relieved the following year by the same means. The dictionary enters Alkmaar for the means. The Dutch broke their own dykes and drowned their own farmland to save a town, which is a decision of a particular kind: they gave up the ground they lived on because they judged something else to be worth more.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dyke as a bank to confine water; a sluice as a gate to stop or let out water; and inundation as the overflowing of land by water.
webster_full: DYKE, n. [Sax. dic.] A ditch; a channel for water; a mound of earth or stone to confine water and prevent inundation.
SLUICE, n. [Fr. ecluse.] A frame of boards or planks to stop or regulate the flow of water; a flood-gate.
INUNDATION, n. [L. inundatio.] An overflow of water, or other fluid; a flood; the overflowing or covering of land with water.
SIEGE, n. [Fr. siege.] The setting of an army around or before a fortified place to compel it to surrender.
ASSAULT, n. [L. assultus.] An attack or violent onset; in war, an attempt to take a fort or town by scaling walls and entering.

corruption_summary: North Holland town, the first siege the Spanish army failed to carry, relieved in October 1573 by flooding the surrounding polders.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the national myth: the proverb about victory beginning at Alkmaar used as a self-congratulation, with the fall of Haarlem a few months earlier and the cost of the flooding both left out. The dictionary keeps the whole: Haarlem held longer and fell, the farmers whose land was drowned were not the burghers whose town was saved, and a deliverance is not less a mercy for having been paid for by somebody.

The principle to recover is the counting of a cost. Opening the sluices was a deliberate preference of one good over another, and the men who did it knew what they were giving up. “We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks” (Isa 26:1) is the kind of word a besieged town reads, and the dictionary notes that it transfers the confidence from the walls to God, which is precisely what a people must do when they decide that their own fields are expendable.

pos: n. (city of Holland on the Old Rhine; relieved from siege in 1574 and given the first university of the Republic in 1575)
etymology: Dutch Leiden, earlier Leithon, from a Germanic root for a watercourse or channel; the city stands where the Old Rhine divides.
biblical_def: Leiden was a cloth city on the Old Rhine, and its siege is the central episode of the Dutch revolt. The Spanish army invested it in 1573 and again in 1574; the city was reduced to famine and plague and lost a great part of its population; and in October 1574 it was relieved when the States broke the dykes, flooded the land between the city and the sea, and brought a fleet of flat boats up over the drowned fields with provisions. The prince of Orange offered the city a reward, and the city asked for a university. It was founded in 1575, the first in the northern Netherlands, and it became within a generation one of the great universities of Europe and the chief theological faculty of the Reformed world outside Geneva—which also made it the place where the Arminian controversy was fought, since Arminius and Gomarus held its chairs together and the quarrel that produced the Synod of Dort was in large part a quarrel between two Leiden professors. The dictionary enters Leiden for the sequence, which is worth noticing: a city that had been starved asked for a school, and the school it got gave the Reformed churches both their best theological training and their most dangerous controversy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a siege as the setting of an army before a fortified place; famine as scarcity of food; and a university as a corporation for instruction in all branches of learning.
webster_full: SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.
FAMINE, n. [L. fames.] Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions sufficient to cause distress.
UNIVERSITY, n. An assemblage of colleges established in any place, with professors for instructing students in the sciences.
PROFESSOR, n. One who publicly teaches any science or branch of learning; an officer in a university.
CONTROVERSY, n. A disputation, particularly in writing; a dispute concerning a matter of opinion.

Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.
Pro 4:7
Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: Holland city relieved in October 1574 by flooding the land, which asked for a university as its reward and got the Reformed world's chief faculty and its chief controversy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption which came out of Leiden is the Remonstrant doctrine, and the dictionary names it as the Synod of Dort named it: a denial of unconditional election, of the definite atonement, of the effectual call and of the certainty of perseverance, which puts the decisive movement in salvation in the will of the creature. The dictionary holds the Canons of Dort and the 1689 Confession on all five heads, and holds that the controversy was not a misunderstanding between colleagues but a difference about whether salvation is of the Lord.

The principle to recover is that a theological faculty is a danger as well as a gift, and that both follow from the same cause. A university exists to examine questions, and a church that founds one has asked for its doctrine to be examined; the examination will sometimes produce an Arminius and sometimes a Gomarus, and the church's remedy is not to close the school but to hold a synod. “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) is what Dort did, and the contending was possible because the doctrine had been stated clearly enough to be contradicted clearly.
